title: Data Analysis Design by Example
text:
Overview
The best way to learn design in any field is to study examples. These lessons therefore build small versions of real data analysis pipelines to introduce some fundamental ideas in data science and show how experienced data scientists think.
Greg Wilson is a programmer, author, and educator based in Toronto. He was the co-founder and first Executive Director of Software Carpentry and received ACM SIGSOFT’s Influential Educator Award in 2020.

start where you are · use what you have · help who you can

title: 1  Introduction
text:
This book teaches introductory data science by building small versions of real analysis pipelines.
A data analysis pipeline is a chain of small, checkable steps.
The main stages are ingest, clean, explore, model, and communicate.
Ingest: get raw data into a form the computer can read.
Clean: fix types, missing values, and inconsistencies.
Explore: summarize and visualize to see what the data contains.
Model: fit a statistical or computational model to answer a question.
Communicate: report findings so others can trust and reuse them.
Each stage produces something the next stage can consume.
We study examples rather than memorize functions.
Examples teach judgment, like when a technique fits and when it fails.
Memorized functions fade; worked pipelines show how pieces connect.
The book uses two running examples that share the same data shapes.
Matching shapes means code and ideas transfer from one example to the other.
Example one: disaster management, a volunteer emergency-response group.
Its tables are responders and incidents, plus a time series called readings.
The responders table records id, name, joined, and role.
The incidents table records id, timestamp, latitude, longitude, kind, severity, status, and responder_id.
Incident kind is one of storm, flood, power-outage, or fire.
Incident status moves from reported to triaged to dispatched to resolved.
The readings series records timestamp, station_id, river_level, rainfall_mm, and wind_speed.
Example two: ecological data collection, a field survey.
Its tables are sites and observations, plus a time series called environment.
The sites table records id, latitude, longitude, and habitat.
The observations table records id, site_id, species, count, mass_g, length_mm, and date.
The environment series records date, site_id, temperature_c, and pollution_ppm.
Both examples pair a small static table with a larger event table and a time series.
We use mature tools instead of rebuilding them.
The tools are Polars, DuckDB, Vega-Altair (imported as altair), httpx, and doit.
Mature tools are tested, documented, and faster to learn than custom code.
Reproducibility means recording every step.
A reproducible analysis can be re-run from raw data to final result.
Recording steps also lets others audit and correct the work.
Each lesson later in the book turns one stage of a pipeline into a small, runnable example.

title: 2  A Records Generator
text: 2.1 Writing rows

title: 2  A Records Generator
text:
CSV is our exchange format: plain text, no database required, readable by every tool in this book.
A tiny helper turns a list of dictionaries into a CSV file with a header.



The header row records the schema, so the file is self-describing.
newline="" stops Windows from inserting stray blank lines.

title: 2  A Records Generator
text:
2.2 The parent tables

A parent table holds the entities that records will refer to.
responders is the parent for the disaster example: people, each with an ID, a name, a join date, and a role.



sites is the parent for the ecology example: survey locations, each with an ID, a position, and a habitat.



Both parents use a plain integer ID as the join key.
The generator documents its assumptions: the coordinate ranges pin both examples to south-eastern Australia, which would otherwise be hidden magic.

title: 2  A Records Generator
text:
2.3 The records tables

A records table holds many rows per parent row; the foreign key column points back at the parent.
incidents belongs to the disaster example: each row is one report, tagged with the responder who handled it.



observations is the ecology analogue: each row is one species sighting at one site.



observations.site_id mirrors incidents.responder_id: one foreign key column, same role in both examples.
Note how make_observations consults the site’s habitat to pick a plausible species; that is an assumption the generator makes explicit.

title: 2  A Records Generator
text:
2.4 Putting it together

Generate the parent tables first, then the records that reference them.
Writing the files is just four calls to the helper.



CSV is portable: these four files can be opened in Polars, DuckDB, a spreadsheet, or another language without any special tooling.

title: 2  A Records Generator
text:
2.5 Verify the join

Read the files back and join each records table to its parent to confirm the foreign keys line up.
Polars makes the two joins one-liners, and shows the shared shape clearly.



A left join keeps every record and attaches the matching parent row.
If any foreign key had no match, the parent columns would be null; a clean run shows none, so the generator is internally consistent.
Because the data is synthetic, we know the right answer before any analysis: the counts, ranges, and relationships above are the ground truth.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.1 Make a sample
Build a small end-to-end exploratory pipeline over incident records: generate a sample, ingest it, clean the obvious problems, summarize it (incidents per kind, severity distribution), and plot the result. Along the way, meet the two tools this course leans on for exploratory work: Polars for dataframes and Vega-Altair for charts.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
A fixed seed makes the pseudo-random sequence reproducible, so this lesson runs the same every time and the numbers below can be checked against the output.
Generate the sample inline so the lesson is self-contained; a real pipeline would read this from a file or an API instead.



The coordinate ranges pin the incidents to south-eastern Australia, the same region the full generator uses; that is an assumption written down rather than hidden in the code.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.2 Ingest

Ingest brings raw records into a dataframe. Here we round-trip through CSV so read_csv is the ingest step; an API or a database would substitute for the file.
head shows the first rows; the schema it prints is the contract the rest of the pipeline relies on.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.3 Clean

Cleaning is its own lesson; this synthetic data has little to fix, so profile first: check the types and count missing values.
The one real clean-up is parsing timestamp from a string into a datetime, so ordering and date arithmetic work later.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.4 Explore

select picks columns; filter picks rows. Both return a new frame and leave the original untouched.




high.shape is the number of rows and columns: the filter keeps only the most severe incidents.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.5 Summarize

group_by plus an aggregation collapses many rows into one row per group.
Count per kind is the headline number: which incident type is most common?



The severity distribution is the same operation on a different column.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.6 Reshape

pivot spreads one column’s values across the columns, turning a long table into a wide one. Here the severity counts become a matrix with one row per kind.



A null cell means no incident of that kind had that severity; the row and column totals are the summaries computed above.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.7 Communicate

Altair turns a summarized frame into a chart with one declaration: encode the x and y channels and the notebook renders it.
kind is nominal (N) so each value is a separate bar; len is quantitative (Q) so bar height is a measured value. sort="-y" orders the bars tallest first.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
3.8 Check the answer

Every pipeline ends by checking its answer against something known. The synthetic data gives us ground truth: the counts must sum to the number of rows, and every kind must appear.



The ecology twin runs the same stages with observations grouped by species, so “count per kind” becomes “count per species” and the chart labels species on the x axis; only the column names change.

title: 4  Data Dictionaries and Provenance
text:
4.1 The data dictionary
Build the metadata layer of a pipeline: a data dictionary that records each field’s name, type, units, meaning, and allowed values, and a provenance log that records each step’s inputs and outputs.

title: 4  Data Dictionaries and Provenance
text:
A data dictionary has one row per field, with columns for the name, type, units, meaning, and allowed values.
The incidents table is the running example; the dictionary below documents its eight fields.
The allowed values for a categorical field are the controlled vocabulary for that column: nothing else may appear.
Writing those vocabularies as constants means the dictionary and the validation code share one source of truth.



Store the dictionary as a list of dicts first; a list is easy to read and edit, and every other tool can import it.
A categorical field stores its allowed values as a list; a numeric field stores a description of its range; None means the field is not constrained.



Turn the list into a dataframe so the dictionary renders as a table and can be queried. This is the point of “metadata is data”: the dictionary is just another table.
Lists do not display well in a cell, so join them into a comma-separated string for display and keep the original list for validation.



Because the dictionary is a table, ordinary dataframe queries answer questions about the data without touching the data itself.

title: 4  Data Dictionaries and Provenance
text:
4.2 The dictionary is a contract

The producer promises to write values the dictionary allows; the consumer relies on that promise. The dictionary is the written contract both sides read.
Validation turns the contract from a promise into a check: walk the categorical fields and flag any value outside the controlled vocabulary.



A few hand-written rows stand in for the producer’s output. Two values break the contract on purpose: "Flood" is capitalized and "critical" is not a severity in the dictionary.




The two violations are the contract doing its job: without the dictionary, "Flood" and "critical" would silently become separate categories in every downstream summary.

title: 4  Data Dictionaries and Provenance
text:
4.3 Provenance

The dictionary records what each field means; provenance records where each result came from.
A provenance log is a sequence of records, one per transformation step, each naming the step, its inputs, its outputs, and when it ran.
Appending one small dict per step keeps the log simple and machine-readable.



Run a small pipeline over the incidents and log each step. The log is the audit trail that links the final summary back to the raw rows.



Write the log as JSON lines: one JSON object per line, easy to append and easy to read back with any tool.



Reading the log back as a dataframe closes the loop: the metadata layer is itself queryable data, so you can ask “what were the inputs to the summary?”




Without this log, a summary is a rumor: you cannot say how it was made or re-make it.
The dictionary says what the data means; the log says where it came from. Together they are the metadata layer that makes a pipeline reproducible.

title: 4  Data Dictionaries and Provenance
text:
4.4 The ecology twin

The observations table needs the same treatment; only the fields differ.
Units matter more here: mass_g is grams, length_mm is millimeters, and count is a number of individuals.

title: 5  A Data Cleaning Pipeline
text:
Build a cleaning pipeline over raw incident records for the disaster-management example: profile the data, deduplicate it, normalize labels, fill missing values, and validate the result, then emit a clean table and a small quality report. The same stages apply to the ecology example (normalize species names, drop repeated observations).

Cleaning is a pipeline of small, testable transformations, not one big fix.
Profile first: types, ranges, and missingness tell you what to fix.
Deduplication needs a definition of “same record”.
Record the effect of every change so clean data can be traced to raw data.

We fix the random seed so the dirt we inject below is the same every run, which makes the pipeline reproducible and testable.

Generate forty plausible records. Real data arrives this way from an ingest step; here we synthesize it so the lesson is self-contained.

Inject dirtiness, as if several sources wrote to one shared log. Each line is a separate defect, and each defect gets a distinct fix later.

Profile before fixing. Types, shape, missingness, ranges, and label counts tell us what is broken and how much of it there is.

Deduplicate next. “Same record” is a decision, not a property of the data: if the same event can be logged twice under a new id, identity is the event’s content, not its id. We key on kind, place, and time.

Normalize the labels: lowercase everything, then map synonyms to one controlled value. A tiny helper makes the rule reusable and testable on its own.

Fill missing severity with an explicit policy: a missing severity means “not recorded”, so we mark it unknown rather than inventing a value or dropping the row.

Validate the result against the rules we care about. Location is essential, so rows that cannot be placed (null or outside the study bounds) are dropped, and every categorical value must be in its controlled set.

Emit the two outputs: the clean table and a quality report. The report is the audit trail: each count records what a stage changed, so clean data can be traced back to raw data. In a full pipeline you would write clean to Parquet and the report to JSON for the next stage to read.

title: 6  A Time-Series Generator
text:
6.1 The decomposition
Build a generator that produces a daily time series for either running example: river level for the disaster example, or temperature and pollution for the ecology example. The series is trend plus seasonality plus noise plus one injected anomaly, so the monitoring and forecasting lessons have a known target to find.

title: 6  A Time-Series Generator
text:
Import the tools this lesson needs. math and random come from the standard library; polars holds the data and altair draws it.
Pin the seed first so the series is identical on every run.



A time series decomposes into three parts. The trend is the slow, long-run movement. The seasonality is the repeating cycle. The noise is the random jitter on top.
Real data only hands you the sum; a generator lets you set each part and see how they combine.
We name the components as constants so the recipe reads like the model it encodes.

title: 6  A Time-Series Generator
text:
6.2 A daily river series

A river gauge records one number per timestamp. We synthesize two years of daily readings for the disaster example’s readings table.



The level at day t is the base plus a linear trend, a sine wave that repeats every 365 days, and Gaussian noise.
A flood is a brief excursion: on one chosen day we add a large jump, then the series returns to its usual shape.
We tag that day in an anomaly column so later lessons have a labeled target, not just a story.



The timestamp is a real calendar date, one day apart, so the plot and any date arithmetic behave like real monitoring data.
anomaly is the ground truth: it says which point is unusual, so a detector can be scored against it.
A real readings row also carries rainfall_mm and wind_speed; we generate only river_level here, and the other columns follow the same recipe.

title: 6  A Time-Series Generator
text:
6.3 Plot the series

Draw the series and drop a red mark on the injected flood.
The trend and season are the slow rise and the yearly wave; the noise is the fuzz; the flood is the lone spike.



The red dot sits exactly on the injected point, because we put it there.
A detector that flags that point is right; one that misses it or flags the noise is wrong, and we can measure which because we know the truth.

title: 6  A Time-Series Generator
text:
6.4 The ecology twin

The same recipe maps to the ecology example by renaming the columns and the units.
temperature_c carries the seasonal cycle; pollution_ppm is a flatter baseline with its own injected spike.
A real environment row keys each reading to a site_id; here we generate one site’s series.



The temperature series is a seasonal wave around a fixed mean; the pollution series is a flat baseline with a single spike.
Plot pollution to see the same injected-anomaly shape in a different unit.



The spike stands out from the baseline exactly as the flood did, so the monitoring lesson’s target exists in both running examples.
Because the seed is pinned, every number above is fixed: run the notebook again and you get the same series, the same spike, and the same plot.

title: 7  A Cohort and Retention Pipeline
text:
A cohort shares a defining event; retention tracks its members over time.
Grouping activity by cohort and period is a self-join.
Retention answers “do they come back?”, not just “how many started?”.
For the disaster example the members are volunteers and the activity is an incident response; for the ecology example the members are sites and the activity is a survey.
The defining event is a choice. Here it is a volunteer’s first response, not their sign-up month, because signing up is not the same as showing up.



Start with two helpers that move between "YYYY-MM" labels and integer month numbers. An integer makes “months since first response” a subtraction.



Generate the two tables with a fixed seed so the lesson is reproducible. A volunteer has a joined sign-up month; an incident records one response at a timestamp.



joined records when a volunteer signed up and can precede their first response, which is why the cohort is derived from the incident log instead of trusted from joined.



Convert each response’s timestamp to an integer month so later arithmetic is a plain column difference.



Join each response to its volunteer to carry along the name, role, and sign-up month. Then take each volunteer’s earliest response month: that is their cohort.



The cohort assignment is computed from the same records it is then joined back onto, which is why this is a self-join. period is months since a volunteer’s first response: zero means “their first month”.



Group by cohort and period and count distinct volunteers active in each cell. Rows are cohorts, columns are periods.



Check against a property that must hold: a cohort’s period-0 count equals its size, because every member responded in their first month.



Counts answer “how many?”. Dividing each cell by its cohort size answers “what fraction?”, which is a retention rate.



Plot the matrix as a heatmap. Reading down a column shows one cohort aging; reading across a row shows the same period for different cohorts.
crumbs: 7  A Cohort and Retention Pipeline

title: 8  A Funnel Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that traces records through an ordered sequence of stages and reports the drop-off at each one. For the disaster example the stages are reported → triaged → dispatched → resolved (the status field); for the ecology example they are surveyed → identified → vouchered → published. A distinct kind of analysis: funnel and conversion analysis.

A funnel orders stages and measures conversion between them.
Each stage is a filter; drop-off is the complement of conversion.
Funnels reveal where a process loses records.
Stage order changes the answer, so write the order down before you read the numbers.

Start with the tools and the fixed stage order.


A seed makes the pseudo-random sequence reproducible, so this lesson runs the same every time and the numbers below can be checked against the output.
Each incident has one status: the furthest stage it reached. To make later stages progressively fewer, walk each incident forward and let a fixed fraction fall off at each step.



Grouping by status and counting gives a histogram of final states, not a funnel. A funnel counts every record that reached a stage, and a record that reached a later stage also passed through the earlier ones.
Give each stage an integer position, then count how many records reached a stage by summing the final-status counts from that stage onward.



cum_sum(reverse=True) adds the counts from the last stage back to the first, so reached at reported is all incidents and reached at resolved is only the survivors.
Conversion is the share that moved from one stage to the next; drop-off is the share that did not. They add up to one.



The last stage has no next stage, so its conversion and drop-off are null.
Plot the funnel as bars ordered by stage, with the reached count labeled on each bar.



The funnel shows the biggest drop-off is between dispatch and resolution (about 40%), then between triage and dispatch (about a third), so those are the transitions worth investigating first.
The answer depends on stage order: “reached triaged” assumes every triaged, dispatched, or resolved incident passed through triage. If a record can skip a stage, or two stages are not strictly sequential, the cumulative count is wrong.
Check the result: the first stage’s reached equals the total incident count, and conversion + drop_off is 1 for every stage that has a next one.

title: 9  An A/B Test Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that compares two variants (e.g., two alerting strategies for disaster response, or two sampling protocols for the field survey) with a permutation test and a bootstrap confidence interval for the effect size. A distinct kind of analysis: experimentation and inference.

An experiment compares two variants of one thing, holding everything else fixed.
Here the question is whether two alerting strategies differ in how fast people respond.
Variant A is a siren alert; variant B is a text message.
We will simulate response times so the true answer is known, then test whether the pipeline recovers it.
A fixed seed makes the random data reproducible.



Each group has 200 responders, with response times drawn from a bell curve.
Variant A has a mean of 120 seconds; variant B is a bit faster at 110 seconds.
The two curves share a spread of 25 seconds, so the difference is real but not huge.



Put both groups into one Polars dataframe, with a column recording which variant each row came from.



The observed effect is the difference in means, A minus B.
It is just a number; the rest of the lesson asks whether it is real or could be noise.



The null hypothesis says there is no real difference: both groups come from the same distribution.
Under the null, any difference we saw is just random assignment of labels.
A permutation test simulates the null by shuffling the variant labels many times.
Each shuffle recomputes the difference; if the labels do not matter, shuffled differences look like the real one.



The p-value is how often shuffles look at least as extreme as the real data.
A small p-value means the real difference is unlikely under the null, so we reject the null.
A p-value near 0 here is expected: we built in a true 10 second difference.
The permutation test needs no formula for the sampling distribution, which is why it is easy to trust.
A p-value says whether a difference exists, not how big it is.
The bootstrap estimates the effect size with a confidence interval.
Resample each group with replacement, recompute the difference, and repeat to build a distribution of plausible effects.



The middle 95% of bootstrap differences is the confidence interval.
The interval here should sit near the true 10 second gap and exclude 0.
A confidence interval that excludes 0 agrees with the p-value: the effect is real.
The bootstrap works because resampling mimics drawing new samples from the same population.
Permutation and bootstrap both trade many recomputations for assumptions we would otherwise have to justify.
In a real deployment, swap the simulated times for measured response times and re-run unchanged.
The ecology twin is the same shape: two sampling protocols, compared on the counts or masses they produce.
Seed everything, log the p-value and interval, and a colleague can reproduce the whole comparison from scratch.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.1 A synthetic river series
Build a pipeline that forecasts a numeric time series (river level for the disaster example, or population counts for the ecology example) by fitting a simple trend and seasonal model, and judge it by forecasting the held-out recent past. A distinct kind of analysis: prediction over time.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
We need a series whose shape we control, so we generate one: a slow rising trend plus a yearly cycle plus random noise.
The disaster example forecasts river_level from the readings series; the ecology example forecasts population count from the environment series, and the same code runs with the column renamed.
Pin the seed first so the series is reproducible.



A monthly reading over six years gives 72 points.
The level is a base height plus a trend that rises a little each month, a sine wave that repeats every 12 months, and Gaussian noise.
The sine wave is the season: winter highs and summer lows, or any repeating yearly pattern.



t is the month index; the level is everything else.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.2 Hold out the recent past

Backtesting means pretending the last stretch of the series has not happened yet: we fit only on the earlier points and forecast the rest.
The held-out points are the recent past, and they are the honest test: the model never sees them while it is being fit.
We hold out the final year.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.3 A naive baseline

The simplest forecast repeats the last known value for every future point.
It is nearly always wrong, but it gives a floor: a real model should beat it, or the model is not earning its keep.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.4 A trend and seasonal model

A slightly smarter model fits a straight line through the series to capture the trend.
The slope is the average change per month, estimated by least squares; the intercept is where that line starts.



After removing the trend, what is left is the seasonal shape plus noise.
Average the detrended leftovers by month: month 0 gets the mean of every January leftover, month 1 the mean of every February, and so on.
Those twelve averages are the additive seasonal terms.
The spread of the residuals around the fitted pattern, sigma, is our first estimate of the typical error.



Forecasting is just extending the line: for each month ahead, add the trend times that month plus that month’s seasonal term.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.5 Measure the error

Mean absolute error is the average distance between the forecast and the truth, in the units of the series.
We compute it on the held-out points, which the fit never saw.



The trend and seasonal model should beat the naive baseline, because it captures the yearly rise and fall that the naive forecast ignores.
Beating the naive floor is the minimum bar; it does not mean the forecast is good.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.6 Plot actual vs forecast

Altair draws the actual held-out points and both forecasts on the same axes.
The closer a forecast line sits to the actual line, the smaller its error.



The naive line is flat, so it misses the seasonal curve entirely.
The trend+seasonal line bends with the season, so it tracks the actual values much more closely.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
10.7 Forecast uncertainty

A point forecast is a single number; a useful forecast also says how sure we are.
sigma from the training fit is a first estimate of the typical error.
A rough interval is the forecast plus or minus two sigma: about 95% of values should land inside if the errors are normal and independent.



The interval widens as we forecast further ahead, because each step adds new uncertainty.
For the naive model the error accumulates like a random walk, so its interval grows with the square root of the horizon.
A constant band is a simplification; a real pipeline reports a band that widens with the horizon.
The ecology twin forecasts population count the same way: generate a trend plus seasonal series, hold out the recent past, fit the naive and trend+seasonal models, and compare their MAE.
Rename the column and adjust the units, and the pipeline runs unchanged.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.1 The Model
Build a least-squares regression pipeline: fit a line to predict a numeric outcome (e.g., response time from a disaster’s severity and distance, or organism mass from pollution and length) then inspect the residuals, and evaluate the fit on held-out data. A distinct kind of analysis: predictive modeling with a continuous outcome.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
Regression predicts a numeric outcome from numeric features.
The disaster example predicts an incident’s response time in minutes.
Two features drive that response: the incident’s severity and its distance.
We assume the relationship is linear: response = w0 + w1*severity + w2*distance.
w0 is the intercept; w1 and w2 are slopes, the extra minutes per unit of each feature.
The ecology example uses the same shape: mass = w0 + w1*pollution + w2*length.
Our job is to estimate the three coefficients from data, not to assume them.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.2 Generate Synthetic Data

We make data with known coefficients so we can check the fit against truth.
A fixed seed makes the data reproducible: the same numbers on every run.
Each row is one incident: a severity from 1 to 5, a distance in kilometres, and noise.
Noise stands for everything the model does not capture, like road conditions.
The hidden truth is response = 5 + 3*severity + 0.4*distance + noise.
If the fit recovers numbers near 5, 3, and 0.4, we know it works.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.3 The Normal Equations

Least squares chooses the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
A residual is the gap between an observed value and the value the line predicts.
Squaring makes big errors cost more than small ones and removes the sign.
For a linear model the best coefficients have a closed form called the normal equations.
We solve X'X w = X'y, where X holds a column of ones plus the features.
We build X'X and X'y with plain loops, then solve by Gaussian elimination.
No NumPy: this is the whole idea, written out where we can see it.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.4 Fit and Interpret

The design matrix X has one column per coefficient: ones, severity, distance.
We fit on all the data to see how close the estimates come to the truth.
The intercept is the predicted time for severity 0 and distance 0.
The severity slope means one more severity step adds about 3 minutes.
The distance slope means one more kilometre adds about 0.4 minutes.
These meanings hold only because the relationship really is linear here.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.5 Look at the Residuals

Residuals are the part of the outcome the model did not explain.
Their mean is near zero: least squares balances over- and under-prediction.
Their spread shows how far off the model typically is.
A pattern in residuals, like growing with severity, means the model missed structure.
With synthetic noise the residuals should look random, which is the honest case.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.6 Evaluate on Held-Out Data

A model that fits the data it saw can still fail on new incidents.
Fitting error only measures memorization, not prediction.
We split the data: fit on a training set, score on a test set the model never saw.
The split uses its own seed so the data-generation seed stays fixed.
Mean absolute error is the average size of the prediction error, in minutes.
Training and test MAE should be close; a big gap is a warning sign.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.7 Plot Actual vs Predicted

A plot shows what a single error number hides.
Each point is one held-out incident, actual time on one axis, predicted on the other.
Points on the diagonal are perfect predictions.
Points above the diagonal were over-predicted; below, under-predicted.
A tight cloud around the diagonal means the model explains most of the variation.
A cloud that fans out means the error grows in one direction.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
11.8 Summary

Least squares picks the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals.
The normal equations give that line in closed form, solvable in pure Python.
Coefficients read as “extra minutes per severity step” and “per kilometre”.
Residuals show what the model missed; a clean model leaves random-looking noise.
Never trust a fit on its own training data; score it on held-out incidents.
The actual-vs-predicted plot shows the whole story a single error hides.

title: 12  A Classification Pipeline
text:
12.1 A synthetic incident table
Build a pipeline that predicts a category (e.g., will this incident report escalate, or which species an observation records) from its features, and judge it with a confusion matrix and the right metric. A distinct kind of analysis: predictive modeling with a categorical outcome.

title: 12  A Classification Pipeline
text:
We predict whether a disaster incident escalates from two features: its severity and its kind.
The ecology twin predicts species from an observation’s mass and length; the same code runs with the columns renamed.
Start by pinning the seed, then generate rows.



random.seed makes the generator reproducible: the same seed gives the same rows every run, so a colleague can re-run and check the whole pipeline.



escalated is the label we will predict: 1 means the incident escalates, 0 means it does not.
The chance of escalation rises sharply with severity, and fires escalate more often than power outages, so there is a real signal for a model to find.
The label is imbalanced: most incidents do not escalate.

title: 12  A Classification Pipeline
text:
12.2 Split and fit

Fit on one part of the data and evaluate on the rest, so the score reflects how the model does on rows it has not seen.
The rows are already in random order, so the first 80% and last 20% form a fair split.



Our classifier is a threshold rule: predict escalation when severity is at least some cutoff.
It is crude but transparent, and a real pipeline often starts with a simple rule before reaching for something fancier.



To fit the rule, try each cutoff on the training data and keep the one that best balances precision and recall.
First we need to count the four kinds of outcomes, and turn those counts into scores.



A true positive is an escalation we caught; a true negative is a non-escalation we correctly ignored.
A false positive is a false alarm; a false negative is an escalation we missed.
Precision is the fraction of our alarms that were real; recall is the fraction of real escalations we caught.
F1 is their harmonic mean, a single number that rewards both at once.

title: 12  A Classification Pipeline
text:
12.3 Predict and evaluate

Apply the chosen threshold to the test data, which the fit never saw.



The matrix has four cells: true negatives top left, false positives top right, false negatives bottom left, true positives bottom right.
The diagonal is correct answers; the off-diagonal is two different kinds of mistake.

title: 12  A Classification Pipeline
text:
12.4 Why accuracy alone misleads

Accuracy is the fraction of rows we got right, but on imbalanced data a trivial rule can score well.
A classifier that always says “no escalation” gets every non-escalation right and only misses the rare escalations.



With about a third of incidents escalating, “always no” is right roughly two times in three, yet it catches none of the escalations.
Its accuracy is just the share of the majority class, which is why the number alone is deceptive.
Accuracy hides that failure; recall exposes it.
Which metric matters depends on the cost of each kind of error.
If a missed escalation costs lives, prefer high recall: we would rather send some false alarms than miss one real escalation.
If every alarm sends a crew and crews are scarce, prefer high precision: we would rather miss an occasional escalation than waste a crew.
There is no single best metric; there is a metric that matches the decision the model feeds.
The ecology twin is the same shape: predict species from mass_g and length_mm, and judge the result with the same confusion matrix.
Rename the label, swap the feature columns, and the pipeline runs unchanged.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
13.1 Generate the data
Build a pipeline that finds the records most like a given one (e.g., which past incidents resemble the one just reported, or which survey sites or specimens look like a new one) under a distance on chosen features. A distinct kind of analysis: nearest-neighbor and similarity search.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
Pin the seed first so the pseudo-random stream reproduces exactly.
random.seed makes the “random” numbers deterministic: same seed, same rows.



Each incident has three numeric features: severity, latitude, and longitude.
severity runs 1 (minor) to 5 (major); the coordinates sit in south-eastern Australia, matching the running example.



id labels a row; it is not a feature, because a label carries no notion of closeness.
Text columns would need a different distance, so we leave them out for now.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
13.2 Choose a distance

A distance turns two feature vectors into one non-negative number.
Euclidean distance is the straight-line distance: the square root of the sum of squared differences.
math.dist computes it; the distance is zero only when two rows are identical.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
13.3 Scale the features

severity spans 1 to 5, but each coordinate spans about 10 units.
In raw distance the wider coordinate spread outweighs severity, so severity barely moves the answer.
Standardizing gives every feature the same spread, so each counts equally.



A z-score subtracts the feature’s mean and divides by its standard deviation.
After scaling, every feature has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
“One unit apart” now means “one standard deviation apart” in any feature.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
13.4 Find the nearest neighbors

Take the first incident as the query.
Compute its distance to every row; the query’s distance to itself is zero.
Drop the query row, sort ascending, and keep the k closest.



Nearest neighbors generalize “equal to” into “near to”.
Recommendation (“show me more like this”) and record linkage (“is this the same site?”) both rest on this idea.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
13.5 Scaling changes the answer

Compare the same query in raw and scaled space to see the choice matter.



The two lists differ: raw distance ranks id 8 in the top three, scaled distance puts id 7 there instead.
Which one you use is a decision about what “similar” means for this problem.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
14.1 From text to tokens
Build a pipeline that turns free text (incident report descriptions, or the field notes on an observation) into tokens, counts terms, and scores documents with TF-IDF so the terms that distinguish one report from another stand out. A distinct kind of analysis: text mining.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
Incident reports arrive as free text, not as rows and columns, so the first job is to turn each report into units we can count.
A token is one countable unit, here a single whitespace-separated word.
The ecology twin is the same shape: field notes stand in for report descriptions and run through the same code.
Our tokenizer does three things: lowercase, strip punctuation, and split on whitespace.




Lowercasing turns “Flood” and “flood” into the same token, which is what we want when we count.
str.translate with str.maketrans("", "", string.punctuation) removes punctuation in one pass.
Splitting on whitespace is the simplest possible tokenizer; a real pipeline would also handle contractions, numbers, and domain jargon.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
14.2 Count terms

The simplest summary of a document is how often each term appears, its term frequency.
collections.Counter turns a list of tokens into counts in one call.
Divide each count by the number of tokens so a longer document does not automatically score higher.



d2 and d4 have four tokens, so their frequencies are 0.25 instead of a third; normalizing by length keeps the comparison fair.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
14.3 Down-weight common terms

Term frequency is a start, but “flood” appears in three of five reports and tells us little about any single one.
Document frequency counts how many documents contain a term.
Inverse document frequency (IDF) is high for rare terms and low for common ones: it is the log of total documents over document frequency.




A term that appears in every document has document frequency equal to the total, so its IDF is log(1), which is zero.
Terms unique to one document get the highest IDF, about 1.609 here.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
14.4 TF-IDF

TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency.
A term scores high only if it is frequent in this document and rare in the others, which is exactly what distinguishes one report from the rest.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
14.5 Documents as vectors

A document is now a vector of term weights, one dimension per term.
Most entries are zero because most terms do not appear in most documents.
Gather the weights into a tidy Polars frame, one row per document-term pair, then pivot into a document-by-term matrix.




Pivot spreads the term column into one column per term, and fill_null(0.0) records the terms absent from a document as zero.
The top-weighted term in each document is the one that separates it from the others.



Each document’s top term appears in that document alone, which is why its IDF, and therefore its TF-IDF, is high.
Text needs the same cleaning as numbers: lowercase before comparing, strip punctuation, and decide what to do about typos and near-duplicates.
The ecology twin swaps incident descriptions for field notes and runs the same pipeline unchanged.
A real pipeline would next remove stopwords and stem words; the standard library gives us the counting pieces, and we assemble the rest ourselves.

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.1 Build the data
Build the same analytical workflow we have been doing with Polars, but express it in declarative SQL through DuckDB. The questions are the same; the way we ask them is different.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
We reuse the disaster example: a small responders table and a larger incidents table.
Pin the random seed so every run produces the same rows.



responders has one row per person: an id, a name, a join date, and a role.



incidents has one row per report, with responder_id pointing back at a person.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.2 Load into DuckDB

DuckDB is an embedded database: it runs inside our process, with no server to start.
The schema names each column and its type, which is the contract the rest of the analysis relies on.
We create the tables with SQL DDL, then insert the Polars rows in one batch.
(con.register can attach a Polars or pandas frame directly, but that path needs PyArrow; DDL keeps this lesson dependency-free.)



executemany binds each ? placeholder to a value and inserts the whole batch in one call.
The ISO timestamp strings are cast to real TIMESTAMP and DATE values by the engine.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.3 SELECT and WHERE

SELECT picks columns; WHERE picks rows. Together they are Polars’ select and filter.
SQL names the columns you want; the engine decides how to fetch them.




Filtering is a WHERE clause, and ordering is ORDER BY.




Note the difference in mood: SQL states the condition as one declarative sentence; Polars spells out each step in order.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.4 GROUP BY

Aggregation is GROUP BY: split rows into buckets, then compute one number per bucket.




COUNT(*) is pl.len(), and the alias AS n is .alias("n").
Both engines push the counting into optimized C code rather than a Python loop.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.5 JOIN

A JOIN matches rows in two tables on a shared column, exactly like Polars’ join.
Here we attach each responder’s name to the incidents they handled.




AS gives a table a short alias so column references read clearly.
left_on and right_on are the Polars mirror of SQL’s ON i.responder_id = r.id.
A LEFT JOIN would keep every incident even when a responder id was missing; here every id matches, so inner and left agree.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.6 Aggregating with expressions

Real questions combine operations: count incidents per status and show the average severity.




Same shape, same answer: SQL reads as one sentence, Polars as a chain of verbs.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
15.7 Two mental models

A dataframe and a relational table are two views of the same rectangle of data.
Polars is imperative: you write the sequence of operations to run.
SQL is declarative: you write the result you want and let the optimizer choose the order.
DuckDB’s columnar engine reads only the columns a query touches, which is why it is fast on analytics.
Neither model is universally better; learning both means you can read other people’s code in either style.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
16.1 A mock server
Build a pipeline that ingests storm reports from a web API, transforms the JSON into rows, and loads them into DuckDB, following pagination, a rate limit, and a cache along the way. The disaster twin fetches storm reports; the ecology twin fetches species observations from the same shape of endpoint.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
Real APIs need accounts, network access, and rate limits, so we stand up a tiny HTTP server that serves a fixed payload instead.
The stdlib http.server gives us a handler class and a threaded server.
Running the server in a background thread keeps the notebook responsive.



The payload is six storm reports: one per event, with a severity, a position, and the time it was reported.
We will serve them two pages at a time, the way a real API paginates.



The handler answers GET /reports?page=N with one page of JSON.
The next field is the following page number, or null on the last page, so a client can follow the chain without knowing the total in advance.
log_message is silenced so the request log does not clutter the output.



Bind to port 0 to let the operating system pick a free port, then read the port back from the socket.
The server runs in a daemon thread, so it stops when the process exits.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
16.2 Fetch with a cache

httpx.get is the workhorse: it makes the request and returns a response whose .json() parses the body.
raise_for_status turns a failed request (a 404 or 500) into an exception instead of letting bad data flow silently onward.
A dict keyed by URL is a tiny cache: a re-run returns the stored value and never touches the network.



fetch_count counts only real requests, so we can prove the cache works.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
16.3 Paginate and rate-limit

Follow the next pointer page by page until it is null, collecting every item into one list.
time.sleep between pages is a crude rate limit: a real pipeline would also read the server’s rate-limit headers and back off when asked.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
16.4 Transform

Transform picks the fields we want and puts them in a fixed order, so the loader does not depend on the exact shape of the JSON.
It returns a tuple, which DuckDB can bind directly in an insert.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
16.5 Load into DuckDB

An in-memory database is enough for a lesson; swap the connection string for a file path to persist it.
The schema names each column and its type, which is the contract the rest of the analysis relies on.



executemany inserts the whole batch in one call, binding each ? to a value from a tuple.
The ISO timestamp string is cast to a real TIMESTAMP by the engine.



Now the data is queryable with ordinary SQL.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
16.6 Re-run from the cache

Fetch everything again: every URL is already cached, so no new HTTP request is made.
That matters in a real job, where a re-fetch may cost money or hit a rate limit.



The ecology twin is the same pipeline with a different payload: fetch paginated species observations from iNaturalist or GBIF, transform each record into species, count, latitude, and longitude, and load into the same kind of table.
Only the endpoint URL and the field names change; the fetch, paginate, cache, and load steps carry over unchanged.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 17  An Anomaly and Monitoring Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that flags unusual values and detects drift in a time series (e.g., a flood spike in a river gauge, or a pollution spike at a study site) using z-scores and rolling statistics. A distinct kind of analysis: monitoring and anomaly detection.

An anomaly is an observation far from what a model expects.
Z-scores and rolling statistics define “expected” and “far”.
Drift means the data’s baseline itself is moving.
Monitoring runs continuously, so it must be cheap and logged.
Import the tools this lesson needs. statistics comes from the standard library; polars and altair do the heavy lifting. We fix the seed so the synthetic series, spike, and flags are identical on every run.



A river gauge is a time series: one number per timestamp. We synthesize a week of hourly readings as a flat baseline plus small noise, then inject one brief flood spike. Real data would arrive from an ingest step; here we make it ourselves so the lesson is self-contained.



An anomaly is an observation far from what a model expects. Our first model is “the level is usually the mean, give or take the standard deviation”. A z-score measures distance from that mean in units of standard deviation: zero is average, 3 is three standard deviations out.



Flag any point whose z-score is outside three standard deviations. Taking the absolute value catches both a spike and a sudden drop, since either is unusual.



Only the four spike points clear the threshold; the noise is well inside it. We flag rather than drop: an anomaly is a signal to inspect, not an error to remove.



The plot puts a red dot on each flagged reading, exactly on the spike. But the global mean and standard deviation are fixed. If the river’s usual level slowly rises, “expected” has moved and every new reading starts to look unusual. That movement is drift, and rolling statistics track it.



The rolling version flags only the leading edge of the spike. A window that contains the spike absorbs it into its own mean and standard deviation, so the trailing points look ordinary again. Rolling statistics follow a slow baseline well and catch a single sharp jump poorly. In practice you keep both models: a global one for the usual level and a rolling one for drift.
Monitoring runs continuously, so each check must be cheap. A rolling mean and standard deviation update in constant time from a couple of running sums, and need only the last few readings, not the whole history. Every alert is logged with its readings, window, and threshold, so it can be traced back and replayed.
The same pipeline runs on the ecology example with only the column changed: swap level for pollution_ppm, and a pollution spike at a study site is flagged the same way.
crumbs: 17  An Anomaly and Monitoring Pipeline

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
18.1 Generate the blobs
Build a pipeline that groups records into segments (e.g., incidents by kind and severity, or sites by species composition) with a simple k-means routine and interprets what each cluster means. A distinct kind of analysis: unsupervised segmentation.

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
Import the tools this lesson needs. math and random come from the standard library; polars builds the table and altair plots it. We fix the seed so the synthetic blobs are identical on every run.



Each incident has two numeric features: a kind_code (a numeric encoding of the incident kind) and a severity score. We make four true groups and scatter points around each group’s center with random.gauss, so the data has real structure for k-means to find.



kind_code is a number because k-means works on distances, and distances need numbers. The text label stays alongside for interpretation later.
Plot the raw points to see the structure we are trying to recover. The color is severity, not cluster: we do not know the clusters yet.



Four loose blobs are visible. k-means will recover them from distance alone, with no labels, which is the whole point of clustering.

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
18.2 Implement k-means

A centroid is a point that represents a cluster; a cluster is the set of records closest to its centroid.
Distance is Euclidean: the straight-line distance in the feature space, from math.dist.



Start by choosing k points as initial centroids. Random starting points are the usual choice; fixing the seed makes the start reproducible.



Assignment: each point joins the nearest centroid. Update: each centroid moves to the mean of its members. That alternation is where the name “k-means” comes from.



Alternate the two steps until the assignment stops changing: that is convergence. We cap the loop in case it oscillates.



Turn the two feature columns into a list of points, run k-means with k equal to the number of groups we generated, and attach the result.

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
18.3 Look at the clusters

Plot each point colored by its cluster. The colors are the structure k-means found; they are not yet meanings.



The four colors line up with the four blobs, so the algorithm found the structure we planted. It did not know the group labels; it worked from positions alone.

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
18.4 Interpret the clusters

k-means finds structure, not meaning. A cluster is a set of nearby records; what it stands for is our job to decide.
Summarize each cluster by the kinds it contains and its average severity.



Each cluster has a dominant kind and a severity level, so we can read them as segments: one cluster is mild storms, another is severe fires, and so on. Those labels are the meaning we assign, not something the algorithm returned.
The ecology twin runs the same way: encode each site’s species composition into numbers, cluster the sites, then ask a field biologist whether the clusters match habitat types.

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
18.5 Validate

Validation asks two questions: is the grouping stable, and is it useful?
Stability first. A single random start is a gamble: if two starting centroids land in the same blob, the final split can come out wrong.



The second run’s centroids land in different places, so it found a different grouping. One start is not enough to trust.
The standard fix is to try several random starts and keep the one whose members sit tightest around their centroids. That tightness is the within-cluster sum of squares.



Run several starts and keep the best by that score.



With the best of eight starts, the answer is the same whichever eight starts we draw, so the grouping is stable after all.



We compare sorted centroid positions, not label ids, because the numbering may permute between runs while the geometry stays the same.
Usefulness: ask what a cluster lets you do. The best-of-eight clusters map cleanly onto kinds, so a dispatcher gets segments worth treating differently. If two clusters would be handled the same way, they may as well be one.

title: 19  A Reproducible Pipeline
text:
A pipeline is a directed graph: each step consumes the outputs of the steps before it.
The runner is the program that walks that graph and executes the steps in the right order.
doit is one such runner; Make and Snakemake are two others.
We describe the graph in a file named dodo.py, with one function per step.
Whatever your running example, data/*.csv stands in for its raw tables and report.html for its final summary.



targets names the files a task produces.
file_dep names the files a task needs to read; data/*.csv is a glob that matches every CSV.
actions is the command that turns the dependencies into the targets.
task_report depends on bin/script.py and every CSV, so changing any of them invalidates report.html.
task_make_data declares no dependencies, so it is the source of the graph.
bin/make_data.py writes the two CSVs; bin/script.py reads them and writes report.html.

doit list

doit list prints the task names and their docstrings without running anything.

doit

doit runs every task whose targets are missing or older than its dependencies.
The first run builds everything, from the raw CSVs up to report.html.

doit

Run it again and doit reports that nothing is out of date, so no step re-runs.
Edit one CSV (or bin/script.py) and doit re-runs only the steps downstream of it.
task_report re-runs; task_make_data stays put because its own inputs did not change.

doit clean

doit clean removes every declared target but leaves the source files in place.
The next doit rebuilds the whole graph from scratch.
A runner re-executes only the stale steps: the ones whose inputs changed since their outputs were last produced.
Re-running only stale steps saves time, but it is also the mechanism that makes an analysis reproducible.
The dodo.py file records each step, its inputs, and its outputs, so anyone can re-run the pipeline from raw data to final report.
This is how real tools manage analyses end-to-end: state the graph once, and the runner tracks what to redo for you.
A hand-rolled “run everything again” script is faster to write and slower to trust, because it does not record which outputs came from which inputs.

title: 20  Conclusion
text:
This book built small versions of real analysis pipelines rather than toy examples.
Every lesson paired a pipeline of a different kind with one of two running examples.
The first running example was a volunteer disaster-response group coordinating work.
The second running example was a field survey collecting ecological data.
The through-line: take a real problem, shrink it, and solve it with mature tools.
We used existing, battle-tested tools instead of rebuilding them from scratch.
“Mature tools” meant libraries and programs that already handle the hard edge cases.
Each pipeline covered the same shape: ingest, clean, analyze, report.
The specific techniques changed from lesson to lesson, but the shape did not.
Verify: check your work against a known answer before trusting it.
Document: write down what you did and why, for your future self and for others.
Reproduce: make the whole run repeatable, so results can be checked and built on.
The habits matter more than any single technique in the book.
Tools and libraries change; the practices of verification, documentation, and reproduction do not.
Carry those three habits into whatever analysis you tackle next.
Start small, use what already exists, and leave a trail someone else can follow.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.2 Our Responsibilities
Project maintainers are responsible for clarifying the standards of acceptable behavior and are expected to take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any instances of unacceptable behavior.
Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, or to ban temporarily or permanently any contributor for other behaviors that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.3 Scope
This Code of Conduct applies both within project spaces and in public spaces when an individual is representing the project or its community. Examples of representing a project or community include using an official project email address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event. Representation of a project may be further defined and clarified by project maintainers.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.4 Enforcement
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported by emailing the project team. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated and will result in a response that is deemed necessary and appropriate to the circumstances. The project team is obligated to maintain confidentiality with regard to the reporter of an incident. Further details of specific enforcement policies may be posted separately.
Project maintainers who do not follow or enforce the Code of Conduct in good faith may face temporary or permanent repercussions as determined by other members of the project’s leadership.

title: Appendix C — Contributing
text:
C.1 FAQ
Contributions are very welcome; please contact us by email or by filing an issue in our repository. All contributors must abide by our Code of Conduct.

title: Appendix C — Contributing
text:
Do you need help?

Yes—please see the issues in our repository.

What sort of feedback would be useful?

Everything is welcome, from pointing out mistakes to suggestions for better explanations.

Can I add a new section?

Possibly, but please reach out before doing so.

Why is this material free?

Because if we all give a little, we all get a lot.
